after: ## The Big Three: motives and aims
alt: A spectrum from weakening Germany permanently to avoiding new grievances: Clemenceau (security, reparations, Alsace-Lorraine) on the harsh end, Lloyd George in the middle, Wilson (Fourteen Points) on the mild end. Below, why: France had been invaded twice, while the USA entered late and suffered far less.
caption: Each leader's aims reflected what his country had suffered.

alt: A labelled schematic, not a map. Arrows show land leaving Germany: Alsace-Lorraine and Saar coal to France, Eupen and Malmédy to Belgium, North Schleswig to Denmark, West Prussia and Posen to Poland, Danzig a Free City, Memel taken, a plebiscite in Upper Silesia. Dashed lines mark restrictions: the Rhineland demilitarised and Anschluss forbidden. Germany's army is limited to 100,000. Below: Article 231, reparations of £6,600 million fixed in 1921, and the loss of all colonies.
caption: Germany lost land on every border, its colonies and most of its armed forces.

after: ## Why the victors did not get everything they wanted
alt: A table of what each leader got and did not get. Clemenceau got a demilitarised, occupied Rhineland but no independent Rhineland, and lost his guarantees. Wilson got the League, but not self-determination for Germans or US membership. Lloyd George got colonies and naval limits, but reparations were higher than he thought wise. Below, the deeper reasons.
caption: Conflicting aims and pressure at home meant compromise for all three.

after: ## The impact on Germany to the end of 1923
alt: A timeline from 1919 to 1923 drawn to scale: the Treaty (June 1919), the Kapp Putsch (March 1920), reparations fixed and Erzberger murdered (1921), Rathenau murdered (1922), the Ruhr occupation and hyperinflation (1923) and the Munich Putsch (November 1923). A note: wartime borrowing and the government's choice to print money also played a part, and Stresemann stabilised the currency by late 1923.
caption: Resentment of the Treaty fed four years of political violence and crisis.

after: ## The impact on Germany to the end of 1923
alt: Four steps: Germany falls behind with reparation deliveries in late 1922; French and Belgian troops occupy the Ruhr in January 1923; the government backs passive resistance by printing money; hyperinflation destroys the mark by late 1923, wiping out savings and hitting the middle classes hardest.
caption: Printing money to support resistance in the Ruhr turned inflation into hyperinflation.

after: ## Could the Treaty be justified at the time?
alt: A balance. Justified: Brest-Litovsk, French devastation, the 1871 precedent, and Germany keeping its industry. Not justified: no negotiation, sole blame in Article 231, self-determination denied to Germans, and reparations Keynes thought unpayable. A note: fair by the victors' standards, unfair by Wilson's.
caption: Fair or unfair depends on whose standard you use.
